name: The Partnership Model: Capital, Time, and Profit
description: Understand why a partner’s profit share depends on the capital used and how long it was invested.
script_scope: Define partners and partnership; derive the capital-time measure from profit being proportional to the capital committed and the duration for which it is used. Distinguish simple partnership (equal durations, so capital alone sets the ratio) from compound partnership (different durations, so capital × time is compared). Explain compatible time units, capital units, positive investments, zero-duration boundaries, and why profit shares sum to total profit. Ground in Important Facts and solved examples 1–2, with objective patterns contrasting equal and unequal investment periods.

name: Profit Sharing with Equal Investment Periods
description: Reduce capital contributions to a ratio and allocate a known gain or loss when partners invest for the same duration.
script_scope: For equal investment periods, form the profit/loss ratio directly from capital contributions. Reduce monetary amounts without changing their order, allocate a known total by ratio parts, and find a partner’s share or total from one known share. Include capital ratios given as fractions, percentages, multiples, or differences, and check that allocated shares sum to the stated total. Ground in solved examples 1 and 4 and objective patterns 1–8, 27–28, and 33–35.

name: Capital-Time Ratios for Different Durations
description: Compare investments made for different lengths of time before dividing a partnership’s profit.
script_scope: Calculate each partner’s equivalent capital as capital × duration, then reduce those products to obtain the profit/loss ratio. Handle months, years, and mixed but convertible time units; distinguish the investment amount from the capital-time product. Allocate total profit, find one share, or find the total from a share. Verify by rebuilding the weighted products and checking the shares sum to the total. Use solved examples 2, 7, and 11 and objective patterns 9–18, 36, 42–44, and 54–58.

name: Partners Joining or Leaving at Different Times
description: Build each partner’s active investment period from a shared business timeline.
script_scope: Draw a business timeline, identify the total partnership term, and convert entry or exit dates into each partner’s duration. Use the remaining months (not elapsed months) for a late entrant, and split a year correctly when a partner exits early. Combine each duration with its capital and compare capital-time products. Include two- and three-partner timelines, month/year changes, and a check that durations fit within the stated term. Ground in solved examples 2, 9–11 and objective patterns 10, 12–20, 47–50, and 57–60.

name: Capital Added, Withdrawn, or Reduced During the Business
description: Treat every capital change as a new time segment and total the weighted contribution correctly.
script_scope: Partition the business term at every addition, withdrawal, or partial reduction. For each segment, multiply the amount actually invested during that segment by its duration, then add a partner’s segment products. Handle increases stated as a percentage or fraction of original capital, partial withdrawals, complete exits, multiple changes, and equal dates. Avoid counting the same capital twice and verify the segment durations sum to the business term. Use solved examples 3, 5, 13 and objective patterns 21–26, 29, 37–40, 59–64.

name: Finding an Unknown Joining Time or Investment Duration
description: Use a stated profit ratio to solve when a partner joined or how long capital remained invested.
script_scope: Translate a profit ratio into equality or proportionality of capital-time products. Let an unknown entry time be x months and express the remaining duration as T−x; alternatively let the unknown duration be x and solve from known capital and profit shares. Keep x within the valid business period and check the result by substituting it back into the original ratio. Include equal-profit and unequal-profit conditions, two or three partners, and distinguish joining after x months from investing for x months. Ground in solved examples 10–11, 14 and objective patterns 47–50, 57–58.

name: Finding an Unknown Capital from Profit Shares
description: Recover a missing contribution or initial capital by comparing its weighted share with known partners.
script_scope: Set known and unknown capital-time products in the ratio of the partners’ profit shares, then solve for the missing capital. Include an unknown initial contribution when an investment is later increased or reduced, and cases where a partner’s stated share is a fraction of total profit. Check the solved capital is positive and substitute it into the full multi-partner ratio. Ground in solved examples 12–13 and objective patterns 37, 43–45, 49, 51–53, and 64.

name: Allocating Total Profit, Loss, and a Partner’s Share
description: Turn a capital-time ratio into actual rupee amounts and validate the complete distribution.
script_scope: Given partner weights (capital or capital-time), add ratio parts, find the value per part from the total gain/loss, and calculate individual shares. Reverse the process when one share is known, and use gain or loss consistently as the distributable amount. Distinguish share ratio from actual rupee share, preserve currency units, and check all amounts sum to the stated total. Ground in solved examples 1–7 and objective patterns 2–9, 13–18, 31, 36, and 42.

name: Recovering a Total or Partner Share from a Difference
description: Use the difference between profit shares to find an unknown total, capital, or contribution.
script_scope: Represent each share as its ratio fraction of the total and translate a stated difference into an equation. Solve for total profit, an unknown investment, or the difference between capitals while retaining the correct capital-time weights. Avoid subtracting ratio terms before confirming both shares use the same total. Verify by computing the individual shares and their difference. Ground in solved examples 6, 7 and objective patterns 11, 28, 32, 40, 46, 51.

name: Working Partners and Management Allowances
description: Separate a working partner’s agreed management payment from the profit shared by investment.
script_scope: Distinguish a working partner’s management remuneration from a sleeping partner’s investment-only share. Calculate an agreed fixed amount or percentage of total profit first, subtract it from the distributable remainder, then divide that remainder in the capital or capital-time ratio; add the allowance back to the working partner’s final receipt. Check total receipts equal total profit and clarify the stated base for any percentage. Ground in solved example 6 and objective questions 31 and 42.

name: Special Profit-Sharing Agreements
description: Handle equal divisions, capital-based portions, and charitable deductions before allocating the remainder.
script_scope: Translate an agreement into ordered pools: first remove a charity percentage or management allowance if specified; divide an equal portion equally; then allocate the remaining portion by capital or capital-time weights. Keep percentages based on the stated total unless the wording defines another base. Include mixed equal-and-proportional distributions, return on capital, and a check that every pool is allocated exactly once. Ground in objective patterns 7, 30–32, and 56.

name: Rent and Shared-Resource Costs by Usage
description: Allocate a shared rent or expense according to each partner’s time, occupancy, or equivalent resource use.
script_scope: Allocate common rent or costs in proportion to the relevant usage measure, such as people or animals × time, or occupancy over successive periods. For different resource types, first convert them to a common equivalent only when the problem supplies a valid equivalence (for example, relative feed consumption); then multiply by duration. Explain why unused periods are not charged to departed users, and verify shares sum to total rent. Ground in solved examples 7–9 and objective patterns 4 and 36.

name: Building Capital Ratios from Relationships
description: Translate fractions, percentages, multiples, and linked conditions into a common capital ratio.
script_scope: Represent linked capital conditions with a common variable, clear fractional denominators, and derive a consistent multi-partner ratio before applying duration. Handle statements such as one partner investing a fraction of another, a fixed difference, equality of combined contributions, or equivalent expressions such as 4A=6B=10C. Distinguish capital ratio from profit ratio when durations differ. Check the derived ratio against each original condition. Ground in solved examples 4–5 and objective patterns 8, 27–30, 33–35, and 45–46.

name: Multi-Stage and Multi-Year Partnership Accounting
description: Combine several partners, changing capitals, and different timelines without losing track of any segment.
script_scope: Solve partnerships with three or more partners, multiple years, staggered entry/exit, and several capital changes. Build a timeline ledger per partner, split at every event, calculate all capital-time segments, and then form the profit ratio. For multi-year profit questions, use the full stated term and express durations consistently. Check every segment is represented once and recompute the final ratio independently. Ground in solved examples 3, 5, 13–14 and objective patterns 16–26, 29, 37–40, 59–64.

name: Integrated Partnership Reasoning and Data Sufficiency
description: Choose and combine partnership methods, then decide whether statements provide enough information for a unique answer.
script_scope: Integrate capital-time ratios, staged changes, unknown shares, and mixed agreements in fresh problems requiring a deliberate sequence of methods. For data sufficiency, test each statement alone, then both together; distinguish a unique numerical answer from a ratio-only result, identify redundant statements, and detect when information remains insufficient. Preserve the chapter’s answer-choice logic for two- and three-statement questions and justify every sufficiency conclusion algebraically. Ground in the chapter’s Data Sufficiency Questions 1–13 and mixed objective patterns.
